findings.evidence: phrase: "Regulators opened a probe into top AI companies over safety risks." — but the source (Ars Technica) frames the FTC probe as being about whether "security incidents harmed Americans" (data-breach-style failures, fine them "on par with companies that delay data breach reports"), not general AI safety risk.
findings.suggestion: Change 'safety risks' to something matching the source's actual accusation, e.g. 'over security incidents' or 'over data-breach-style failures', so the nature of the accusation isn't broadened.

findings.evidence: phrase: "Days later, a government leader's own edited photo was flagged as AI-made" — the two sources are published the same day (2026-10-15, 15:43 and 21:09 UTC), roughly six hours apart, not 'days later'.
findings.suggestion: Remove the invented timeline or replace with something the sources support, e.g. 'That same week' or no temporal claim at all.

findings.evidence: alt text: "a government official proudly holds up a framed photo of a stone column" — this specific detail (a photo of a stone/White House column, flagged as AI-edited) matches only one known real-world incident, making the otherwise-unnamed 'government leader' unmistakably identifiable as a specific real person.
findings.suggestion: Replace the column-photo prop with a generic, non-identifying image (e.g. a generic landscape or document) in both the alt text and the art, so the figure can't be pinned to one real official by the specific prop.
